newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Another Taiwan firm applies to set up China bank.
newsitem.headline: Another Taiwan firm applies to set up China bank.

text.p: A second Taiwan firm is applying to set up a bank in Shanghai, defying a Taiwan government ban on investments in China, a Chinese central bank official said on Tuesday.

"We are reviewing a Taiwan company's application for the establishment of another Taiwan-invested commercial bank in Shanghai," visiting Chinese official Di Weiping told reporters in Yangmei outside Taipei.
Di, vice president of the Shanghai branch of the People's Bank of China, said the second Taiwan firm, like the first, was new to the banking business.

He declined to identify the latest applicant but said any Taiwan firm with investments of over US$100 million was eligible to apply to operate a banking business in Shanghai, the only place in China that admits overseas-invested banks.
Di confirmed that China recently had approved a Taiwan company's application to set up the first Taiwan-invested bank in Shanghai -- First Sino Bank.

First Sino is a Taiwan-China joint venture with registered capital of US$100 million, he said. The Taiwan side has invested US$80 million in the venture with Shanghai Pudong Development Bank, he said.
Taiwan media have identified First Sino's backer as Pou Chen Corp, a major investor in mainland footwear. Pou Chen officials reached by Reuters declined to comment.
Di is on a 12-day visit to Taiwan with a group of senior Chinese economic officials. They arrived on March 5.
He said First Sino would be allowed to operate a domestic yuan currency business, which would include desposits and loans, once it earns two consecutive years of profits.
Before that, it can engage in business only with foreign or Taiwan-invested companies, he said.
Shanghai has designated Pudong, across the Huangpu River from the city's famous waterfront Bund, as a national financial centre and is using administrative means to speed development.
Taiwan's government has warned local enterprises against investing in China's banking sector, saying all such investments remain banned under longstanding government policy.
Taiwan has maintained a policy of no direct contact with China since a civil war split them in 1949. In the late 1980s, however, it began allowing indirect trade and investment on the mainland.

Officials of the Economics Ministry's investment commission acknowledged it would be difficult to punish First Sino's Taiwan financiers because they are making the investment through offshore subsidiaries.

"The investor had not applied for an approval from us for its mainland project and it will be difficult for us to check, especially when the funds were not remitted from Taiwan," a commission official said.
Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$30 billion on the mainland through third areas since the late 1980s.
